This is Tally. Do their numbers match? By Mia. An entry for the A.I. and Epistemics sprint.

Political speeches lean on numbers. Growth is up. Inflation is down. Each of those numbers comes from an official release, so each one can be checked. But for Nigeria, nobody has put the claims and the official figures side by side in a form others can audit. So the question is simple. When Nigerian leaders quote a statistic, does it match the official figure?

I chose five national addresses before doing any checking. Four by the President, and one by the main opposition candidate, so both sides go through the same procedure. Fifty-nine figures were listed. Thirty-three were checked against the statistics bureau, the central bank, the debt office and others. Thirty-one could be scored. Every scored row has a verdict and a link to its source.

About three in four matched. Twenty-three figures matched the official release, five were close, and three did not match. Every specific growth rate and inflation rate quoted in the five speeches matched exactly.

The biggest miss was a swapped definition. The President said non-oil exports are now forty-eight percent of exports. The official trade release shows crude oil at about fifty-three percent. But another thirty-four percent is other petroleum products and gas. Truly non-oil products were about thirteen percent. The forty-eight percent is everything except crude, and most of that is still oil and gas.

The other errors were more ordinary. A stock market gain quoted from ten days earlier. An oil baseline that belonged to the month before. And the errors ran both ways. Of seven with a clear direction, four helped the speaker and three hurt. Two claims fit no verdict at all. Two official sources give different foreign investment figures, and one debt ratio has no published source.

Can you trust the verdicts? I ran two independent checks. First, a script with no A.I. in it downloaded every source and looked for the recorded numbers. It found all of them in twenty-six of thirty-one rows, and the quoted figures in the rest. Second, a different A.I. model coded every row blind. It agreed on twenty-two of thirty-one, and its match rate was seventy-one percent against seventy-four. So the match rate holds. The line between close and mismatch does not.

What you get is an open dataset, with a source link on every scored row, and a small test set for claim-checking tools in a setting they rarely see. It is small. No human has checked every row. And it does not compare the two speakers. The data, the report and a guide for judges are in the repository. Thank you.
